Received 10 October 2024 l Revised 5 February 2025 l Accepted 17 February 2025 l Published online 11 June 2025 Abstract: Objective: This study examines the drug price negotiation process in China from 2017 to 2023, with a particular focus on its impact on drug pricing, especially for innovative therapies, and its influence on healthcare affordability and the sustainability of the health insurance system. Material and Methods: Data were sourced from public reports and official announcements by the National Healthcare Security Administration (NHSA). A mixed-method approach was employed, combining quantitative analysis of price reductions, success rates, and healthcare expenditure with qualitative insights into policy challenges, focusing on high- cost treatments like oncology drugs and innovative therapies. Results: From 2017 to 2023, price negotiations led to average reductions of 50-62%, with oncology drugs experiencing a maximum price reduction of 94%. The efficiency of negotiations improved significantly, with a success rate of 85% by 2023. These reductions enhanced access to costly treatments, particularly cancer therapies, but rising demand for innovative treatments continued to strain the healthcare budget. The inclusion of more high-cost therapies in the National Reimbursement Drug List (NRDL) further contributed to the growth in expenditure. Additionally, the proportion of domestically produced drugs in negotiations increased from 39% in 2021 to 69% in 2023, reflecting efforts to enhance self-sufficiency. Conclusion: Negotiations on drug prices in China have effectively reduced drug prices and improved access to critical therapies, such as innovative and life-saving treatments. JSON: Name: china_drug_price_negotiation_pipeline Title: Mixed-methods longitudinal econometric evaluation of centralized drug price negotiations' impact on negotiated drug prices and national health insurance sustainability in China (2017–2023) Short Hypothesis: Centralized NHSA-led price negotiations conducted between 2017 and 2023 caused average negotiated unit prices to decline by at least 50% and did not produce a net decrease in annual national health insurance expenditure due to increased utilization and inclusion of high-cost therapies. Related Work: Prior approaches to controlling pharmaceutical spending combine centralized bargaining, health-technology-assessment (HTA)-informed pricing, value-based pricing, and differential reimbursement. In many high-income settings, HTA and value-based frameworks align prices with clinical benefit but require detailed outcome and cost-effectiveness data; centralized bargaining has been used to rapidly lower prices but may not incorporate downstream utilization and budget-impact dynamics. Existing studies on China report large negotiated price reductions and improved patient affordability, and descriptive analyses document catalog adjustments and rising participation by domestic manufacturers. Limitations of current work include: a predominant focus on unit-price effects without rigorous causal links to aggregate fund sustainability; reliance on pre/post descriptive statistics rather than causal inference methods; sparse incorporation of utilization, catalogue-entry selection bias (non-random selection of drugs for negotiation), and demographic demand-side drivers; limited mixed-methods integration to explain mechanisms; and short-term windows that do not quantify medium-term budget impacts or counterfactuals. Abstract: This research pipeline proposes a mixed-methods longitudinal econometric evaluation to quantify the causal impact of China’s centralized drug price negotiations (2017–2023) on negotiated drug unit prices and national health insurance sustainability. Using a cleaned panel of drug-level pre/post prices, sales volumes, NRDL entries, NHSA announcements, aggregated claims and national insurance fund income/expenditure, we will estimate causal effects with difference-in-differences, interrupted time-series, synthetic control and fixed-effects regressions while integrating qualitative policy-document coding. The main contribution is an end-to-end workflow that links negotiated price changes to utilization, payer spending, and catalog composition, producing robust point estimates, counterfactual forecasts, and mechanism insights (selection, domestic substitution, and utilization responses). Expected outcomes include quantified price-reduction elasticities, budget-impact estimates, sensitivity to therapeutic area (e.g., oncology), and policy-relevant evidence on whether negotiated price reductions alone are sufficient to secure long-term fund stability. Experiments: Datasets: (1) NHSA public negotiation announcements and NRDL lists (2004–2023); (2) drug-level list price and negotiated price time series (2017–2023); (3) monthly/quarterly sales and volume data at product level (2017–2023) from public procurement and commercial databases; (4) aggregated hospital/insurance claims or reimbursement totals by drug category and month (2017–2023); (5) national health insurance fund income/expenditure and surplus ratios (2018–2023); (6) insurance enrollment counts (active/retired) and demographic controls; (7) registry of domestic vs imported origin and therapeutic class metadata. Baselines: (A) simple pre-post comparisons; (B) interrupted time series (ITS); (C) difference-in-differences (DiD) using non-negotiated but clinically similar drugs as controls; (D) synthetic control applied to cohorts of negotiated drugs; (E) fixed-effects panel regression with drug and time FE. Primary outcomes and metrics: percent change in unit price (mean, median), negotiation success rate, change in treated patient counts (utilization rate per 100k), change in aggregate payer spending (RMB/year), budget impact (cumulative RMB saved or spent), active-to-retired ratio, surplus ratio, RMSE for forecasts, and p-values/95% CIs. Experimental setup: construct balanced panel with pre-intervention window of ≥24 months and post-intervention window ≥24 months where possible; estimate DiD: ΔY_it = α + βTreatment_it + γX_it + μ_i + τ_t + ε_it, clustering SEs at product or manufacturer level; implement event-study specifications to inspect dynamic effects; estimate ITS on national spending series with segmented regression. Ablation/robustness studies: (1) exclude oncology drugs; (2) restrict to domestically produced drugs; (3) drop years 2020–2021 to test pandemic confounding; (4) use alternative control groups (therapeutic subgroups); (5) alternative outcome definitions (unit price vs total spending). Additional checks: placebo interventions, falsification outcomes (therapeutic areas not subject to negotiation), and sensitivity to covariate inclusion. Qualitative component: code policy documents and NHSA statements into categories (pricing mechanism, selection criteria, negotiation rules) and map timeline to quantitative shifts. Risk Factors and Limitations: Data quality and coverage: public and commercial sources may have missing, inconsistent, or proprietary data gaps (prices, volumes, claims). Selection bias/endogeneity: drugs chosen for negotiation are not random; unobserved confounders (anticipated demand, clinical breakthroughs) may bias causal estimates. Policy simultaneity: concurrent reforms (NRDL expansions, reimbursement rule changes, pandemic responses) create attribution challenges. Measurement error: list price vs actual transaction price and rebates may differ. Temporal confounding: short post-intervention windows for some drugs limit detection of medium-term effects. Generalizability: findings specific to China’s institutional and regulatory context and may not transfer to other countries. Model risks: misspecification of econometric models and overfitting in synthetic control or forecasting components. Interpretability limits: inability to observe firm-level profitability or R&D investment effects directly. Computational constraints: large panel with many products and monthly granularity may require substantial compute and memory for some estimators.
